hints: Integrate a to get v(t), then integrate again for the displacement over 0 to T, and divide by T.
worded:
1. The acceleration is not constant, so average velocity must come from displacement ÷ time.

2. v(t) = a₀(t − t²/2T), reaching ½a₀T at t = T.

3. Displacement = area under v(t) = a₀(T²/2 − T²/6) = a₀T²/3. Average velocity = a₀T/3. (A)

4. Sense check: the v–t curve is concave (rises quickly, then levels off), so the average lies above the simple ¼a₀T of a straight line through the origin to ½a₀T; ⅓a₀T fits.
conventional:
![](asset:P000157-sol-1)

$$v = \int_{0}^{t}a_{0}\left( 1 - \frac{t}{T} \right)dt = a_{0}\left( t - \frac{t^{2}}{2T} \right).$$

$$\Delta x = \int_{0}^{T}a_{0}\left( t - \frac{t^{2}}{2T} \right)dt = a_{0}\left( \frac{T^{2}}{2} - \frac{T^{2}}{6} \right) = \frac{a_{0}T^{2}}{3},\quad\quad\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{T} = \frac{a_{0}T}{3}.$$
mistakes: ½a₀T (option B) is the final velocity, not the average.
